title: Capex or opex? Classifying property maintenance spend
summary: Classifying property maintenance spend as CapEx (capital expenditure) or OpEx (operating expenditure) hinges on whether the work extends the asset’s useful life, enhances its value or capability, or simply keeps it in its current operating condition.
body_markdown:
A maintenance invoice lands on your desk. Is it an operating expense or a capital expenditure? For a property business, that answer can affect this year’s profit, your balance sheet, depreciation, and potentially your tax position. If you manage spend across multiple properties,[spend management for real estate groups](https://www.alaan.com/industries/real-estate) can also help you keep the right context attached to each expense.


The definitions are simple enough. OpEx covers the costs of keeping a property running, such as routine repairs, maintenance, and utilities. CapEx covers spending that improves an asset or extends its useful life, such as a major renovation or replacement.


The difficult part is knowing where the line sits. A repaired chiller is straightforward. A replaced chiller? That depends. Here’s how to classify property maintenance spend with more confidence.


## Understanding the CapEx vs OpEx meaning


If you are wondering what[CapEx and OpEx](https://www.uschamber.com/co/run/finance/capex-opex-and-cogs-explained) are, the simplest way to look at it is this: CapEx improves or adds to an asset, while OpEx keeps it running. That is the basic CapEx vs OpEx meaning you need to know before classifying a property expense.


- Capital expenditure (CapEx) is spending on acquiring an asset or improving an existing one in a way that provides future economic benefits. It is recorded on the balance sheet and generally recognised as an expense over time through depreciation.
- Operating expenditure (OpEx) covers the costs of running and maintaining a property. Routine repairs, servicing, utilities, and management fees are typical examples and are generally recognised in the profit and loss account when incurred.


Here’s a quick look at the difference:


CapEx OpEx


Improves or adds to an asset Maintains or operates an asset


Recorded on the balance sheet Recorded in the profit and loss account


Generally recognised over time through depreciation Generally expensed when incurred


Major renovation, new HVAC system, roof replacement Routine servicing, minor repairs, cleaning, utilities


## How to tell if property spend is a repair or an improvement


The hardest CapEx vs OpEx decisions usually come down to one question: does the spending simply restore an asset, or does it improve the asset or extend its useful life?


Under[IAS 16](https://www.ifrs.org/premium/) , day-to-day servicing and repairs are generally recognised as expenses when incurred. Costs that meet the recognition criteria for an asset, including qualifying replacement components, are capitalised instead. Here are four common CapEx vs OpEx examples for UAE property businesses:


- Routine servicing: OpEx. Servicing an HVAC system, carrying out preventive maintenance, or replacing minor worn parts keeps the existing asset operating. It does not normally create a new asset or additional future economic benefits.
- Like-for-like replacement: Usually CapEx. Replacing a major chiller with a new chiller may be capital expenditure because the replacement is a significant component of the property’s equipment. However, the facts matter: the accounting treatment should reflect whether the replacement meets IAS 16’s recognition criteria.
- An upgrade that extends useful life: CapEx. Replacing an old HVAC system with a more efficient, higher-capacity system, or carrying out work that materially extends an asset’s useful life, is more likely to qualify for capitalisation because it provides future economic benefits beyond routine maintenance.
- A fit-out: Usually CapEx. Spending on a new tenant fit-out, such as installing permanent partitions, flooring, electrical systems, or other significant improvements, will generally be capitalised when it meets the asset recognition criteria.


The key is not the size of the invoice alone. Look at what the work changes about the asset, and whether it creates future economic benefits.


## Setting a capitalisation threshold


A capitalisation threshold is the minimum value at which your business considers an expense for capitalisation rather than immediate expensing. It helps your finance team apply a consistent approach across maintenance spend.


There is no one-size-fits-all threshold for UAE property, facilities management, or construction businesses. The right amount depends on your assets, transaction volume, and accounting policy.


Keep your accounting threshold separate from UAE Corporate Tax rules. The[Federal Tax Authority (FTA)](https://tax.gov.ae/DataFolder/Files/Guides/CT/CT%20General%20Guide%20-%20EN%20-%2010%2009%202023.pdf) governs tax deductions, while your accounting policy determines how costs are recognised in your financial statements. An accounting CapEx or OpEx classification does not automatically determine its tax treatment.


Understanding which[deductible and non-deductible expenses](https://www.alaan.com/blog/deductible-non-deductible-expenses-uae-corporate-tax) apply under UAE Corporate Tax can help you assess the tax implications of your property spend. What matters most is having a documented policy and applying it consistently. Your policy should explain:


- The threshold: the minimum amount at which an expenditure is considered for capitalisation.
- What qualifies: whether the spend must also meet the relevant asset recognition criteria.
- How replacements are treated: particularly for major components of buildings and equipment.
- How grouped costs are handled: several related items may need to be assessed together rather than individually.
- Who approves exceptions: especially for unusual or significant property projects.


A threshold should not become a shortcut for classification. An AED 10,000 repair does not automatically become CapEx simply because it crosses your internal limit. The nature of the expenditure still matters under your accounting policy and IAS 16.


## Common property maintenance costs: CapEx or OpEx?


The following CapEx vs OpEx examples give you a practical starting point. The usual treatment is not automatic: the nature of the work, the asset involved, and whether the expenditure creates future economic benefits can change the classification.


It is also useful to understand how these costs fit into broader[tax-deductible expense categories](https://www.alaan.com/blog/top-tax-deductible-business-expense-categories) when assessing their potential UAE Corporate Tax impact.


Property spend Usual treatment When it could change


HVAC servicing OpEx Significant component replacement


Minor plumbing repairs OpEx Major replacement or new asset


Light bulbs and minor electrical parts OpEx Major electrical upgrade


Painting OpEx Part of a qualifying renovation


Flooring replacement Usually OpEx Major refurbishment or improvement


Like-for-like chiller replacement Usually CapEx Assess against IAS 16 and your policy


HVAC upgrade CapEx Routine repair with no added benefit


Lift modernisation Usually CapEx Routine servicing or minor repairs


Roof repairs Usually OpEx Qualifying major roof replacement


New roof installation CapEx Minor patching or routine repair


Tenant fit-out Usually CapEx Routine repairs or reinstatement


Major renovation CapEx Individual work may still be OpEx


Security system repairs OpEx New CCTV or access-control system


Generator servicing OpEx Major component replacement or new generator


Pest control and cleaning OpEx Part of a qualifying capital project


The accounting treatment is only part of the picture. For significant property spend, you also need to consider how the cost is treated for UAE Corporate Tax and whether it affects your[tax deductions on business expenses](https://www.alaan.com/blog/business-tax-deductions-guide) .


## Get CapEx and OpEx classification right at the point of spend


The easiest time to classify a property expense is when the purchase happens, not at year-end. By then, finance may be looking at a vague invoice that says “maintenance work” and trying to work out months later whether it was a repair, replacement, upgrade, or part of a larger project.


Keeping this information documented from the start also makes an[audit of purchases](https://www.alaan.com/blog/audit-of-purchases) easier. Finance can trace the expense back to the original purchase, supporting documents, property or project, and the reason for its classification. Capture the relevant detail at the source. Your purchase request or expense workflow should make it clear:


- What was purchased or repaired?
- Which property, building, or project does it relate to?
- Is it routine maintenance, a replacement, or an improvement?
- Which asset or component is affected?
- Does the spend form part of a larger project?


This is where[accounting automation](https://www.alaan.com/products/accounting-automation) can take some of the manual work out of the process. Capturing, coding, and matching expense information as it comes in gives your finance team a cleaner record to review, rather than leaving them to reconstruct the details at month-end.


## Final thoughts


Getting CapEx vs OpEx right is less about memorising definitions and more about capturing the right context. Look at what the spend does to the asset, apply your capitalisation policy consistently, and keep the supporting details from the point of purchase.

## FAQs


#### 1. What are some examples of CapEx and OpEx?


CapEx examples include a new HVAC system, a major roof replacement, a significant lift upgrade, or a property fit-out that creates future economic benefits. OpEx examples include routine HVAC servicing, minor repairs, cleaning, utilities, and regular maintenance. The right treatment depends on the nature of the expenditure and whether it meets the relevant recognition criteria under IAS 16.


#### 2. Are employee salaries CapEx or OpEx?


Usually, salaries are OpEx. However, employee costs directly attributable to constructing or bringing a qualifying asset into use may be capitalised under IAS 16.


#### 3. What falls under OpEx?


OpEx covers the day-to-day costs of running and maintaining a property. This includes routine repairs, servicing, cleaning, security, utilities, and management fees.


#### 4. Is a replacement CapEx or OpEx?


It can be either. A significant replacement that meets IAS 16's capitalisation criteria may be CapEx, while a minor replacement made as part of routine maintenance is generally OpEx.


#### 5. Where should you set a capitalisation threshold?


There is no universal threshold for UAE property businesses. Set an amount that fits your business, document it in your accounting policy, and apply it consistently.
